verdicts.corrected_text: The pinned-memory budget of this host is about 14.5-15.0 GiB (14848-15360 MiB). cudaMallocHost gave 14848 MiB in 512 MiB chunks and refused the 30th; it gave 12288 MiB in 4 GiB chunks. The CUDA host buffer type caps buffers at 4 GiB (ggml_backend_cuda_host_buffer_type_get_max_size), so the buffer is split into about 5 chunks (4037/4000/4032/4032/3174 MiB), and a chunk whose cudaMallocHost fails falls back to a pageable CPU buffer. The failure is logged only at debug level, and the multi-buffer keeps the first chunk's CUDA_Host name. With this budget the 4th chunk (about layers 24-33) falls back and the others pin, about 15.2 GiB or 79% of the buffer. The CUPTI copy sizes agree: all pageable expert copies are q5_K slices, and no q6_K copy from layers 34/38/39 is pageable. So --load-mode none is about 80% pinned (warm 37.93 ms, between addr15000 at 39.17, or 38.77 for r2 alone, and prof15000 at 36.43). It takes about 15 s to load instead of 6.3-7.5 s and is not a full-pinning arm.

verdicts.problems: The direction of the memory result holds; the window, the numbers and the mechanism do not. (1) Window. The figures come from analyze.py paging(): the median of the last 60% of typeperf rows. That is not the warm phase. I aligned typeperf rows with token times from the sqlite captures (TARGET_INFO_SESSION_START_TIME plus the logits DtoH copies). The last 60% includes 8-14 rows after the last token, with 14-21 GiB available while nsys exports. It also includes rows from before token 387. Taking only rows from token 387 to the last token, the medians are addr15000 243 / 814 MiB and prof15000 1764 / 2336 MiB, against the stated 284/850 and 1904/2505. Those stated figures only reproduce with the flawed definition. (2) Confirmed parts. low_addr15000_r1.txt says 'lowest available 205 MiB, KILLED: below 300 MiB for 20 s', typeperf has a minimum of 216, and the run stopped at about 840 tokens. Pinned memory was the same: 14946.38 against 14923.83 MiB (log_*15000_*.txt). (3) Mechanism. The gap already exists at the first decode token: available was 1484 / 2221 MiB for addr15000 against 2737 / 3429 for prof15000, about 1.2 GiB. It widens over tokens 3-386 (addr -52/-65 MiB/s, prof -46/-53 MiB/s). In the warm window it shrinks: prof15000 loses memory faster (slope -20.9 / -23.8 MiB/s, 0.73-0.83 MiB/token) than addr15000 (-4.9, held down by the floor near 216 MiB, and -9.3 MiB/s, 0.18-0.34 MiB/token). In r2 the gap goes from 1685 MiB at token 387 to 1396 MiB at the end. Decode page reads/s overlap (addr 731/359, prof 275/460). The 7842 arms show the same pattern: profile order starts decode higher (7853/8388 vs 5852/6946) but declines faster in the warm window (-51 vs -24/-31 MiB/s). The none arm stays flat (about 0 MiB/s), so the decline comes from mmap pages entering the working set. Profile-order pageable experts are therefore not faulted in less often during the warm phase. They enter later and keep entering. The address-order pageable layers, which hold popular experts, are faulted in during prefill and the first about 400 tokens. Whether the gap survives a longer run is open. (4) Minor. 'Normal rate' is confirmed: layers 32-39 hold 3814/18760 = 20.3% of expert bytes and take 21.1% of pooled missed bytes (coverage_2048_runcaps.json layer_share), and 20.2% of upload bytes are pageable measured. But 3814.09 MiB is 3.72 GiB, not 3.8 GiB.
verdicts.corrected_text: Memory: over tokens 387 to the last token (typeperf rows while llama ran), addr15000 had a median 243 / 814 MiB available, and one rep (r1) was killed by the watchdog (below 300 MiB for 20 s, lowest 205 MiB). prof15000 had 1764 / 2336 MiB at the same pinned size (14946 vs 14924 MiB). The 284/850 and 1904/2505 figures come from the last 60% of all typeperf rows, which includes 8-14 rows after the process exited. The gap, about 1.2 GiB, is already there at the first decode token and is built during load, prefill and the first about 400 tokens. In address order the pageable 3.72 GiB are whole layers 32-39, used at the normal rate (21% of missed bytes), and their popular experts are faulted into the working set early. In profile order the pageable experts are the rarely selected ones, so fewer of them have been touched by a given point. In the warm window profile order brings new pages in faster (0.73-0.83 vs 0.18-0.34 MiB/token), so the gap is shrinking, and these 1024-token runs do not show whether it persists.

Every unit then has use 0, so the code pins single experts in address order (thousands of registrations instead of 50-96) and logs '(0 selections)' at INFO. The comment at 761-763 says 'empty if the trace cannot be read', which is true only when the open fails. For the real profile the parser works: a Python replica of the sscanf/strtoll logic over trace_prompt_{b,c,d}.csv gives 244824 selections, matching smoke_prof15000_lines.txt. It keeps 30603 lines and skips 6 (3 headers, 3 empty), and stays correct when the CRLF '\r' is kept, as when a Windows trace is read on Linux.
findings.fix: After parsing: `if (n_sel == 0) { LLAMA_LOG_WARN("%s: no expert selections in the MoE pin profile '%s'\n", __func__, path); return {}; }`. The whole-tensor path then runs, and the comment's 'empty if' becomes true.

findings.summary: sscanf fills call, n_hit and n_miss only to discard them. The n_ids filter repeats the bare 8 from copy() and never fires on the actual profile.
findings.failure_scenario: The literal 8 here matches `ids.size() <= (size_t) 8*n_expert_used ? stats_small : stats_large` in copy() and the 'ubatch <= 8' log label, so the two can drift apart. In the real profile every one of the 30603 data lines has n_ids == 8, so 0 lines were filtered and the branch is untested. Portability is fine: %lld and %n work on MSVC, GCC, Clang and MinGW (libstdc++ enables ANSI stdio). CMakeLists.txt:81-83 defines _CRT_SECURE_NO_WARNINGS on WIN32. sscanf is already used in src/llama-quant.cpp:485 and src/llama-model-loader.h:56, and <fstream> in src/llama-quant.cpp. One limitation: std::ifstream(const char *), like the existing fopen trace writer, takes ANSI paths on Windows, while src/llama-adapter.cpp:433 and src/llama-mmap.cpp:88 use ggml_fopen for UTF-8 paths.
findings.fix: `long long il, n_ids; int off = 0; if (sscanf(line.c_str(), "%*lld,%lld,%lld,%*lld,%*lld,%n", &il, &n_ids, &off) != 2 || off == 0 || ...)`. Assignment suppression with ll is standard and works on all three compilers. Add `static constexpr int64_t max_small = 8;` next to max_batch and use it in both copy() and the parser, or drop the filter. Optionally open the file with ggml_fopen for UTF-8 paths.

findings.summary: merge_ranges does not follow the file's helper idiom. Its call site copies a vector it never uses again. Page rounding and the host_bufts filter are duplicated, and the pair type is spelled out 8 times.
findings.failure_scenario: The file's free helpers are `static` functions with the llama_moe_cache_ prefix at namespace scope (llama_moe_cache_layer_experts:255, _same_layout:265, _is_host_weight:277, _page_size:283), but merge_ranges is a static member of impl. Line 693 `merge_ranges(ranges)` copies the vector by value. The host_bufts std::find check and the base/end page rounding appear at both 680-688 and 822-828. `unit::addr` only breaks ties, and `const ggml_tensor * t = layers[il].experts[0]` is rebuilt for every expert in the inner loop (~808).
findings.fix: Move it to `static std::vector<std::pair<uintptr_t, uintptr_t>> llama_moe_cache_merge_ranges(...)` beside llama_moe_cache_page_size and call it with std::move(ranges). Add one small helper or lambda for page rounding plus the host-buffer check, and use it at both sites. Add `using range = std::pair<uintptr_t, uintptr_t>;` in impl. Hoist t out of the inner loop. Optionally drop addr: units are pushed in (il, e) order, so std::stable_sort on use alone gives layer/expert order for ties, which is address order for a layer-major GGUF.

findings.summary: ranges_by_use charges each expert's page-rounded slices against the cap separately, so the boundary page shared by adjacent experts is counted twice and the cap is underused.
findings.failure_scenario: All expert tensors start off-page, so neighboring pinned experts share a page that is charged once per expert, then deduplicated by merge_ranges. Registered amounts: 14923.83 MiB at cap 15000 (76 MiB unused; log_prof15000_r1.txt), and 7943.22 MiB at the default cap of about 7964 MiB (coverage_2048_runcaps.json key '7964'; about 21 MiB unused). coverage.py pin_experts uses the same per-unit charge, so the offline model and the C++ code agree. The cost is small but undocumented.
findings.fix: Either state it in the comment ('charged per expert, an upper bound once neighbors merge') or charge only the pages not already taken by the previous unit.

issues.summary: ABBA cancels a linear time drift in the arm means. It does not cancel the r1/r2 effect seen here. The arms called 'stable' in C7 are also the ones run closest together in time, so their stability cannot be credited to having no pageable traffic.
issues.evidence:
Recomputed from runs.json, the wall_*.txt files and the pre_*.txt files.

Warm (387-1022) r1-r2 difference by arm, with the time between reps and the change in pre-eviction available RAM (dAvail):
- off: +1.40 ms, 25.5 min apart, dAvail +1442 MiB
- addr7842: +1.71 ms, 20.6 min, +1502 MiB
- prof7842: +1.32 ms, 15.8 min, +605 MiB
- addr15000: +0.81 ms (partial window; +0.47 on the matched 387-839), 11.0 min, +1029 MiB
- prof15000: +0.46 ms, 6.9 min, +552 MiB
- none: +0.41 ms, 2.3 min, +390 MiB

Correlations: time gap vs r1-r2 r=0.91; dAvail vs r1-r2 r=0.79; gap vs dAvail r=0.86. Position and RAM headroom cannot be separated, and the arms most sensitive to headroom (off, addr7842) sit at the ends of the sequence.

The r1 excess is fault idle that decays with token index, not a constant offset. off slow-copy idle in the warm window is 4.34 ms (r1) vs 1.65 ms (r2). The off r1-r2 difference per 128-token window is 18.8, 9.5, 7.0, 1.8, 2.2, 2.0, 0.3, 0.6 ms. So the drift is a memory-state effect, which a time-linear ABBA model does not describe.

The headroom trend saturates: pre-eviction available by position was 20202, 20140, 20664, 20546, 20923, 20958, 21348, 21475, 21575, 21269, 21642, 21644 MiB. That leaves a residual bias of roughly 0.3 ms against the end arms (off, addr7842). This is small next to the pair differences.

Carry-over also differs between reps. none_r2 and prof15000_r2 followed --load-mode none runs and started with standby 685 and 1018 MiB and free 20450 and 20276 MiB. Every other run started with 19.1-20.6 GiB of standby.
issues.what_to_do: Report the ABBA means as cancelling only a linear trend. In C7, drop the inference that low-pageable arms are inherently stable. To separate state from arm, randomize arm order (or put the pinned arms at the ends) with at least 3-4 reps. Record RAM headroom per run and regress on it. Report per-round pair differences next to the arm means.

issues.summary: The eviction method trims every other process. Those processes page back in during the measured runs, so system-wide disk and paging counters are not llama-only. It also gives this session a different and drifting RAM headroom than EXP-0004.
issues.evidence:
evict.py commits and touches 19456-20992 MiB (info.txt), pushing other processes' working sets to the pagefile. It sleeps only 1 s after releasing. No disk-write or per-process counters were collected.

The none arm has no file-backed expert pages and 0.00-0.01 ms slow-copy idle. Yet, aligned to the nsys token timestamps from paging_none_r1.csv, its warm window (387-1022) shows 0.65 GiB of disk reads, 19183 page reads and 1.04 MiB/token pages input, plus 0.36 GiB after the run. none_r2 warm: 0.10 GiB.

So C7's 'time-integrated disk reads 21.3-23.7 GiB per run' includes non-llama I/O. The whole-file read itself is real, though: 19.6-21.1 GiB is read before prefill ends in every mmap run.

EXP-0004 ran without eviction at 16.45-18.24 GiB 'free RAM' (EXP-0004/info.txt). EXP-0005's off warm is 52.95 ms vs 56.2 ms there, with slow-copy idle 3.00 vs 6.7 ms. Cross-experiment comparisons therefore mix headroom, procedure and code (the addr arms now also go through the split path).

Attribute disk reads to the llama process. Wait for the modified list to drain after eviction. Compare against EXP-0004 only under matched headroom, or mark such comparisons as cross-session.

issues.summary: Tokens 3-130 are not cold. The whole-file prefetch at load has read nearly all of the model before decode starts. This window measures soft (transition) faults and some re-faults, and their size depends on RAM headroom.
issues.evidence:
Aligning paging_<tag>.csv to the logits read-backs in each sqlite:
- Before the first large host-to-device copy, 15.7-19.2 GiB is read in about 6 s.
- By the end of prefill, 19.6-21.1 GiB of the 20.81 GiB file has been read in every mmap run.
- Disk reads in tokens 3-130 are only 0.04-1.47 GiB (off_r1 1.47, off_r2 0.33, prof15000 0.07/0.04), against about 28 GiB of uploads in the off arm.

Transition (soft) faults in 3-130 are about 8600/token for off, 5100-5200 for addr7842, 4300-4700 for prof7842, 2300 for addr15000 and 700-800 for prof15000; the none baseline is 135-142. Off-arm fast-copy idle rises from 6.07 ms (warm) to 10.37 ms (3-130). That fits soft faults landing in 'fast' copies, which the 1.5 GB/s slow-copy classifier cannot see.

EXP-0004's cold window had 91.7 ms/token of slow-copy idle. Here off 3-130 slow-copy idle is 15.22 ms (r1 25.4, r2 5.0).

If a truly cold decode is wanted, it needs no whole-file prefetch (or a flushed standby list after load), which is a different experiment.

issues.summary: Load-time memory pressure, the very mechanism C8 proposes, was not measured: typeperf stalls for about 5 s during the load. The 'lowest avail' column mixes load transients with decode-phase lows.

In the first 2 s of each mmap run, available memory drops sharply in one 1-second sample while the disk reads at 2.7-4.0 GB/s: off_r1 6963, prof7842_r2 529, addr7842_r2 990, off_r2 12387 MiB. Split the 'lowest avail' column into load and decode phases. To test eviction during load, measure residency of the first tensors at prefill start, for example by counting hard faults on the first layers' expert copies during prefill per layer.

- ggml-backend.cpp:57-89 splits the buffer at max_size, and line 871 names the multi-buffer after buffers[0]->buft.
- I modeled the split with the 121 tensor sizes in log_off_r1.txt:163-283. The chunks are 4037/4000/4032/4032/3174 MiB.
